publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: By investigating the purchasing of German and French wines we have found that musical ‘fit’ has a profound influence on product choice.

span.label: in-store music priming of product choice
span.quote: Specific musical pieces may activate superordinate knowledge structures4, suggesting how in-store music could influence product choice.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: To test this, four French and four German wines were displayed in a supermarket drinks section.

span.label: Awareness was assessed only by questionnaire self-report, and the authors themselves doubt that this establishes shoppers were genuinely unaware of the influence.
span.quote: Given recent controversy over subliminal perception5 it would be interesting to discover whether they were really as unaware of the effects of muscal ‘fit’ as their quessuggested.

span.label: Only two music conditions were compared; there was no silence control and no music from a non-wine-producing country, and individual differences and shopper indecision were not measured.
span.quote: Future tionnaire research could investigate the effects of music relative to silence, or relative to the effects of music from a country that does not produce wine; the mediating effect of individual differences6; and whether musical ‘fit’ has more influence on product choice when customers are undecided7.

span.label: product choice
span.quote: Specific musical pieces may activate superordinate knowledge structures4, suggesting how in-store music could influence product choice. For example, stereotypical French music should activate superordinate knowledge structures concerning France

span.quote: Specific musical pieces may activate superordinate knowledge structures4, suggesting how in-store music could influence product choice. For example, stereotypical French music should activate superordinate knowledge structures concerning France

span.label: in-store music
span.quote: music affects product choice Royalty payments for non-broadcast commercial uses of music in 1995 amounted to £53.8 million in the UK alone1. Research on music and consumer behaviour2,3 has, however, almost completely ignored the potential effect of in-store music on purchasing and particularly on product choice

span.label: subliminal
span.quote: Given recent controversy over subliminal perception5 it would be interesting to discover whether they were really as unaware

span.label: musical `fit` - the paper's central term, in scare quotes every time it appears and never defined except by its instances: French accordion music with French wine, German Bierkeller music with German wine. A relation between a stimulus and a product's national origin, operationalised entirely by example
span.quote: By investigating the purchasing of German and French wines we have found that musical ‘fit’ has a profound influence on product choice

span.label: priming, as this paper uses it - a verb applied to a PURCHASE, not to a judgement or a reaction time: stereotypical music activates a knowledge structure concerning a country and thereby primes the selection of products from it. The primed thing is which bottle leaves the shop
span.quote: Similarly, stereotypical German music should activate related knowledge and prime the selection of products such as German wines

span.label: unawareness, and the authors' refusal to claim it - only six of the shoppers said the music influenced their choice, and rather than treat that as unawareness established they write that it would be interesting to discover whether they were REALLY as unaware as their answers suggested. A field study declining the unconscious it is entitled to claim
span.quote: Given recent controversy over subliminal perception5 it would be interesting to discover whether they were really as unaware

span.label: in-store music —causes→ product choice
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — The claim in the title, and the design that supports it is a fortnight of alternating days in a real supermarket with the shelf positions swapped halfway - so the effect is on bottles sold, not on stated intention.
span.quote: music affects product choice Royalty payments for non-broadcast commercial uses of music in 1995 amounted to £53.8 million in the UK alone1. Research on music and consumer behaviour2,3 has, however, almost completely ignored the potential effect of in-store music on purchasing and particularly on product choice

span.label: superordinate knowledge structures —causes→ product choice
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — THE MECHANISM, and it is hedged twice in its own sentence - `may activate`, `suggesting how` - so it is offered as the available explanation rather than as something tested. The study measures the outcome, not the structure.
span.quote: Specific musical pieces may activate superordinate knowledge structures4, suggesting how in-store music could influence product choice. For example, stereotypical French music should activate superordinate knowledge structures concerning France

span.label: national background music biases which countrys wine customers buy
span.quote: Similarly, stereotypical German music should activate related knowledge and prime the selection of products such as German wines

span.label: the effect on product choice is measurable in a real store
span.quote: Customers did not seem aware of the effect that music had on their selections.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1038/36484.
